story.headline: Currencies are holding still before US inflation figures at 7:30 AM CT, the last big price check before the Federal Reserve's December 9 decision. Oil kept sliding, with Brent near $91, its lowest since late August.

reads.policy: A December Federal Reserve hike is still the market's main expectation, which keeps rate support under the dollar before today's US inflation figures. Bank of Japan meeting notes showed several members want to hike faster, backing the yen's case for December. Job losses in Canada and New Zealand, and gloomy Australian households, give those banks reasons to wait.
reads.growth: China bought far more from abroad than expected in October, a sign that demand there may be firming, which is mild good news for the Aussie and the kiwi. Australian households, though, are the gloomiest in four years, and Japanese spending is weak. The US job market still looks firmer than Canada's or New Zealand's, a split that favours the US dollar.
reads.inflation: Oil kept falling, which eases fears that the energy shock keeps feeding prices. But Americans still expect prices to rise fast, so today's US figures decide whether the Fed feels more or less pressure. A hot reading would favour the dollar; a soft one would help gold, the euro and the yen.
reads.risk: Stocks held their rebound from last week's AI and chip-stock slump, and hopes of calm in the Gulf kept war fears low. That keeps safe havens like the franc and the yen quiet and leaves the kiwi and the Aussie near Monday's highs. Markets are calm but waiting, since a hot US inflation reading could shake them.
reads.tot: Oil kept sliding to its lowest since late August as President Trump held off on new strikes on Iran and supply looked more plentiful. That cuts the energy bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. It also takes support from the Canadian dollar, which slipped overnight.
reads.positioning: Hedge funds lean toward the dollar and the yen and against the kiwi, the Canadian dollar and the euro, and over the past month they sharply added to their bets against the kiwi and the euro. In the Aussie and the pound, hedge funds and real-money investors sit on opposite sides, with real money betting heavily against both. Monday's jump in the kiwi shows how quickly one-sided bets can unwind.
reads.fiscal: No new budget news overnight. Weak demand at Monday's US three-year bond sale puts today's 10-year sale under watch, since soft buying keeps US borrowing costs high. A Democratic Congress still makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, a mild drag on the dollar.

fed.summary: The Federal Reserve held rates on October 28 with two officials voting to hike. A strong October jobs report has made a December hike the market's main expectation, and today's US inflation figures are the last big check before the decision.
fed.why: US inflation is well above the Fed's 2% goal, Americans expect prices to keep rising fast, and hiring was strong in October. Officials also see the AI building boom adding to price pressure.
fed.watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller speaks at 3:00 AM CT, then US inflation figures at 7:30 AM CT: hot prices would make a December hike close to certain, soft ones would revive doubts. The decision is December 9.

boc.summary: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.50% in October and has said more hikes may be needed. Two months of job losses and falling oil have cut bets on a December hike to about one in three, which weighs on the loonie.
boc.priced: December: hold is the base case; hike about one in three.
boc.why: Dearer energy lifted Canadian inflation, but the job market keeps weakening and oil is now falling. That gives the bank reasons to move slowly.
boc.watch: The summary of the bank's October discussions today at 12:30 PM CT, then oil prices, before the December 9 decision.

rbnz.summary: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand held at 2.75% in October in a 4–3 vote, though members agreed more tightening is likely. Rising unemployment has cut bets on a December hike to below even.
rbnz.priced: December: hike less likely than not.
rbnz.why: Price pressures argue for a hike, but unemployment at its highest since 2015 argues for patience.
rbnz.watch: Whether stocks stay calm, the official election result on November 27, and what the next government means for the budget, before the December 9 decision.

ecb.summary: The European Central Bank held its deposit rate at 2.50% in October, and markets expect a hike in December. Because that hike is already expected, it gives the euro little fresh support.
ecb.why: Euro-area inflation is about double the goal, mostly because of energy, but shoppers are cutting back and borrowing costs have already risen. That makes the bank wary of doing too much.
ecb.watch: President Christine Lagarde speaks Wednesday at 3:45 AM CT and Thursday at 1:30 PM CT, and euro-area growth figures follow Friday, before the December 17 decision.

boj.summary: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% in October, and its meeting notes show several members want to raise rates faster. Markets expect a December hike, which would narrow the gap with other countries that keeps the yen weak.
boj.why: Inflation has been running above the 2% goal, and some members see the rate that neither speeds up nor slows the economy well above today's level. Weak household spending is the main reason others want to go slowly.
boj.watch: US inflation figures today and Japanese wholesale prices on Wednesday at 5:50 PM CT. The decision is December 18.

rba.summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia raised rates to 4.85% on November 3, the highest since 2008, but three members wanted to wait. Australian consumer confidence has since fallen to a four-year low, which supports the case for a pause.
rba.priced: December: no firm pricing yet; the bank itself hinted at a pause.
rba.why: Inflation is still too high, but households are feeling the rate rises and the board is split, so the bank wants to see how its hikes work first.
rba.watch: Australian jobs figures for October next Wednesday at 6:30 PM CT, and the mood in global stock markets, before the December 8 decision.

boe.summary: The Bank of England raised Bank Rate to 4.00% on November 5, its first hike since 2023. Governor Andrew Bailey said it is unlikely to be the last unless the Middle East conflict ends, though falling oil weakens that case.
boe.priced: December: a second hike possible; no firm pricing yet.
boe.why: Energy and fuel costs have pushed UK inflation to its highest in about a year, and several officials want more hikes.
boe.watch: UK growth figures on Thursday at 1:00 AM CT, and oil prices, before the December 17 decision. Cheaper oil would weaken the case for a second hike.

snb.summary: The Swiss National Bank holds its rate at zero and says it can still sell francs if they get too strong. Higher October inflation has made another cut less likely, and markets mostly expect a hold in December.
snb.why: Inflation is low and a strong franc keeps import prices down, so the bank has no reason to hike. October's rise in inflation makes a cut less pressing.
snb.watch: How far the franc moves as war fears ease, and the mood in stock markets, before the December 10 decision.

USD.summary: The dollar sits in the middle of the board: rate and inflation support are partly offset by a Democratic Congress. It held steady overnight as markets waited for US inflation figures, with bets on a December Fed hike still high.

notes.policy: A December Fed hike is the market's main expectation after hiring beat forecasts by a wide margin.
notes.inflation: US inflation is well above the Fed's goal, which keeps pressure on it to keep raising rates.
notes.fiscal: With Democrats controlling Congress, President Trump's spending plans look harder to pass, which trims some support for the dollar.

EUR.summary: The euro sits near the bottom of the board: weak growth, dear energy and France's debt worries outweigh an expected December rate hike. Falling oil has helped it recover a little from its lowest level against the dollar since May 2025.

notes.policy: A December European Central Bank hike is expected, but euro rates still sit below US and UK rates, so the gap works against the euro.
notes.growth: Business surveys and shoppers in the euro area have weakened, with France's economy shrinking again.
notes.inflation: Euro-area inflation is about double the bank's goal, which keeps a December hike on the table.
notes.tot: The euro area buys most of its energy abroad, so dear oil drains money out of the region, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets against the euro in years, so good news could set off a sharp rebound as they close it.
notes.fiscal: France's high debt and shaky budget keep investors demanding extra pay to hold French bonds, which weighs on the euro.

GBP.summary: The pound sits near the top of the board after the Bank of England raised rates to 4.00% and signalled more may follow. Firm business surveys and sticky inflation back that case, though falling oil softens it.

notes.policy: The Bank of England hiked in November, and its governor said it is unlikely to be the last while the Middle East conflict lasts.
notes.growth: UK business surveys have been the strongest since February, even though shoppers have pulled back.
notes.inflation: UK inflation is at its highest in about a year, keeping pressure on the Bank of England.

JPY.summary: The yen sits low on the board because Japanese rates are far below others and Japan pays dearly for imported energy. Its safe-haven pull and a likely December rate hike, which some Bank of Japan members want to speed up, give it some support.

notes.policy: At 1.25%, the Bank of Japan's rate is far below other major banks, even though a December hike is likely and some members want faster rises.
notes.risk: The yen tends to gain when stock markets get scared, as they did last week, and loses some of that pull when they calm.
notes.tot: Japan buys almost all its energy abroad, so dear oil weighs on the yen, though the recent fall in prices eases that.
notes.positioning: Speculators hold one of their biggest bets on the yen in years, which could unwind fast if the mood turns.

CHF.summary: The franc sits in the middle of the board: its safe-haven pull is offset by inflation too low to need higher rates. The Swiss National Bank also says it can sell francs if they get too strong.

notes.inflation: Swiss inflation is low, so the central bank has no need to raise rates from zero.
notes.risk: The franc draws money when markets get nervous, so it supports the franc while the Iran war lingers, even as fear eased this week.

AUD.summary: The Aussie scores well on the board thanks to the highest rates among the major central banks and firm commodity prices. Gloomy households and weak jobs make another hike less likely, and the currency still trades mostly on stock-market mood.

notes.policy: Australia's interest rate is the highest among the major central banks, though the governor hinted at a pause.
notes.growth: Australian unemployment is at a five-year high and consumer confidence at a four-year low, though China's stronger buying helps exporters.
notes.inflation: Inflation is running above the Reserve Bank of Australia's forecasts, which kept it hiking.
notes.tot: Australia sells commodities abroad, and firm prices support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the Aussie, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.

CAD.summary: The Canadian dollar sits mid-board: the Bank of Canada's October hike and oil exports help, but two months of job losses and sliding oil prices have cut bets on more hikes.

notes.policy: The Bank of Canada raised rates in October and says more may be needed, though markets now doubt a December move.
notes.growth: Canada lost jobs in September and October, and growth has stalled.
notes.inflation: Rising costs for Canadian producers point to more inflation ahead.
notes.tot: Canada exports oil, so prices still above last year's support its earnings, though the slide to three-month lows trims that help.

NZD.summary: The kiwi sits low on the board because rising unemployment has cut bets on a December rate hike. It has bounced sharply since an election count pointed to the same government staying, helped by calmer stock markets.

notes.growth: New Zealand's unemployment rose to its highest since 2015.
notes.tot: Firm prices for dairy, New Zealand's main export, and stronger Chinese buying support its earnings.
notes.positioning: Speculators are betting heavily against the kiwi, so better news could set off a sharp rebound as they close those bets.
